analysis.one_liner: Restores the DEA's power to move immediately against drug distributors suspected of fueling the opioid epidemic.
analysis.headline: A bill with 10 Democratic senators behind it to restore DEA opioid-enforcement powers died in the Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2016, Congress changed the Controlled Substances Act to make it harder for the Drug Enforcement Administration to strip a drug company of its registration — the license it needs to ship controlled substances. Companies first had to get a warning and a chance to file a corrective plan, and the DEA had to show an 'imminent danger' before freezing shipments on the spot. This bill would repeal those changes and put the old, faster enforcement rules back in place. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit hard by the opioid epidemic, and the DEA itself, which would regain its pre-2016 speed in suspending or revoking the registrations of distributors and pharmacies shipping suspicious volumes of opioids.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sections of the 2016 law that raised the bar for DEA enforcement, including the requirement that the Attorney General find an 'imminent danger to the public health or safety' before immediately suspending a registration.
Removes the 2016 requirement that registrants be given a chance to submit a corrective action plan before their registration can be suspended or revoked, restoring the DEA's earlier, faster process.
Undoes changes that modified the registration and enforcement authorities of the DEA with respect to manufacturers, distributors, and dispensers of controlled substances.
Restores a 30-day show-cause process under which a registrant must appear before the Attorney General, with proceedings kept separate from criminal prosecutions.

analysis.who_pays: Drug wholesalers, pharmacies, and manufacturers of controlled substances, which would again face immediate DEA suspension of their registrations without a warning-and-corrective-plan period. Some patients could see temporary supply disruptions if a legitimate distributor is caught up in enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the corrective action plan step that currently must precede a suspension or revocation, meaning a pharmacy or distributor could lose its license to handle controlled substances without first getting a warning period to fix the problem.

The 2016 law was titled the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act, and its registration changes were framed as protecting patients' access to controlled medications; repeal could risk interruptions in the supply of legitimate pain and other controlled medications for patients who depend on them.
Repeal restores tougher enforcement on the supply side but does nothing about the demand side of the opioid epidemic — treatment, recovery, and prevention were not addressed in this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is enforcement speed versus due process for licensees. Restoring the DEA's immediate suspension authority directly targets the pipeline of prescription opioids into communities, which is a substantial public-health benefit. The honest cost is that removing the corrective-action window gives legitimate pharmacies and distributors less runway to fix paperwork problems before losing their license, and a small share of patients could face supply hiccups. On balance the bill aimed at a proven harm with a narrow, reversible remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Claire McCaskill introduced the bill on October 16, 2017, joined by Senators Manchin and Hassan.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day.
Nine additional Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors, for 10 total Senate supporters, all Democrats.
No further action appears in the bill's record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug distributors, pharmacies, and manufacturers keep the lighter 2016-era DEA enforcement rules — warning letters and corrective-action periods instead of immediate suspension — because the repeal never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2016 DEA-enforcement amendments.

for.name: Sens. Joe Manchin and Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors when it was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as committee chair but never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on October 16, 2017; no markup, vote, or report appears in its record for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any recorded action either way.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the 2016 changes that made it harder for the DEA to immediately suspend a distributor's registration, requiring an imminent-danger finding and a corrective-action period first. Distributors of prescription opioids would again face on-the-spot enforcement action for suspicious order volumes.

Repeal removes the guaranteed warning-and-corrective-plan step before a registration suspension or revocation, exposing pharmacies to faster DEA action. The 2016 protections were framed as safeguarding patient access to controlled medications.
The 2016 amendments modified DEA registration and enforcement authorities covering manufacturers as well as distributors and dispensers; repeal subjects manufacturers to the stricter pre-2016 rules.
